blocks.text: Verses 7-18 are commonly read with Jeremiah’s first-person laments, often called his “confessions.” Such passages can hold accusation, isolation, protest, an inescapable urge to speak, petition, and despair together. Here the movement from the burning compulsion of verse 9 to the curse on Jeremiah’s birth in verses 14-18 makes the speaker’s anguish especially stark. The precise boundaries of these laments and how directly they preserve Jeremiah’s biography remain disputed.

The received book of Jeremiah brings together poetry, prose sermons, narratives, letters, headings, repeated accounts, restoration collections, oracles concerning nations, and an appendix. Its long compositional and textual history is disputed, but this varied form helps account for why a chapter may move between narrative and intense first-person speech.
